title: Introduction to Computer Science
body:
COMP 1631 is the first programming course in the degree and it assumes no programming
experience. It teaches problem solving in [[Python]]. A problem arrives written in English and
has to leave as a sequence of steps a machine can execute, and working out those steps is the
skill the course is built around. Python is chosen because it hides the machine, so the
attention stays on the steps.

This note is written to be read before any of the others. Each section says what a term means
and links to the note that goes further.

> [!note] The course number changed and this file did not
> This is now **COMP 1701, Introduction to Problem Solving and Programming**, the unified
> first course for Computer Science and Computer Information Systems majors at Mount Royal.
> It replaced COMP 1631 and COMP 1501, which were separate entry-level courses. The folder
> and filename keep the old number because that is the number every existing link points
> at. `COMP 1701` is an alias on this note, so searching for the new number lands here.

## Topics

### What a programming language is

A computer executes [[Machine Language]], which is a stream of numbers that the
[[Processor]] reads one at a time. Each number tells the processor to do something very
small, such as copying a value from one place in [[Memory]] to another or adding two numbers
together. Writing anything useful directly in those numbers is impractical, so a programming
language exists as an intermediate. Source code is text a person writes and a translator turns
into machine language.

There are two ways to run that translation, and [[Interpriting]] against [[Compiling]] is the
distinction that matters immediately. A compiler translates the whole program once and
produces a separate executable file that runs on its own. An interpreter translates and
executes at the same time, one piece at a time. Python is interpreted, so there is no build
step, no executable to hand to somebody else, and the source file has to be present every time
the program runs. It also runs slower than a compiled language, because the translation
happens again on every run. [[Hardware]] covers the components involved, and
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] in second year takes all of this apart properly.

```python
print("hello world")
```

That line is a complete Python program. `print` is a function the language supplies, the text
in quotes is the value handed to it, and running the file causes the text to appear.

### What Python is

[[Python]] is a general-purpose interpreted language. Three of its design decisions account
for most of what a beginner runs into.

It is interpreted, described above. It is dynamically typed, so a variable is a name attached
to a value and the value is what carries the type, which means the same name can be attached
to a number on one line and to text on the next. It uses indentation as syntax, so the spaces
at the start of a line decide which block that line belongs to, and misaligning them changes
what the program does. [[Style Conventions]] is graded in this course for that reason.

Python is also strongly typed, so it refuses to guess across types. `5 + "five"` raises a
`TypeError` and no silent conversion happens.

### Turning a problem into steps

An [[Algorithm]] is a set of steps that is ordered, explicit, effective and complete. The note
carries Polya's four-step method for arriving at one: understand the problem, plan a solution,
implement it, then test and improve. Most of the difficulty in this course is in the first two
steps.

[[Pseudocode]] is the plan written down. It fixes the logic while staying loose about syntax,
so a mistake in the reasoning costs one line of rewriting. A [[Tracing Table]] is the reverse
operation, performed on code that already exists. Execute the program by hand with one row per
step and one column per variable, giving the loop condition a column of its own. It is the
only technique that finds a [[Logic Errors|logic error]], because a logic error produces no
message at all. The course's emphasis on counting loop iterations is a tracing exercise:
work out how many times the body runs, then check that number against what the problem asked
for.

Three planning documents divide the same work by different questions. An [[IPO Diagram]]
records what goes in and what comes out. A [[Structure chart]] records how the functions
divide the problem. [[Program design]] and [[Function design]] cover the full procedure from
problem statement to tested code.

### Variables and data types

A [[Variable]] is a name for a value the program is holding on to. Assignment attaches the
name to the value, and reading the name afterwards gives that value back.

```python
score = 10
score = score + 5      # score is now 15
score += 1             # the same operation, written shorter
```

[[Augmented Assignment]] is that last form, `+=`, and it is worth learning early because
`x = x + 1` reads like a false equation to anyone arriving from a mathematics class. As a
Python statement it means take the current value, add one, and attach the name to the result.

A [[Data type]] is the kind of thing a value is, and it determines which operations make
sense. The four to know first are the [[Integer]] for whole numbers, the [[Float]] for numbers
with a decimal point, the [[String]] for text, and the [[Boolean]] for a value that is either
`True` or `False`. In Python the value carries the type and the name does not, so nothing
objects to a name changing type. That is convenient while writing and it means a mistake goes
unreported until the line that breaks actually executes, which is the argument for
[[Test Coverage]].

[[Input]] and [[Output]] are how a program communicates with the person running it. The trap
specific to Python is that `input()` always returns a [[String]], even when the person typed
digits, so [[Type casting]] to `int` or `float` has to happen before any arithmetic.

```python
age = input("How old are you? ")     # age is the text "20"
age = int(age)                        # age is now the number 20
```

Forgetting that conversion is the first real bug most students write.

### Comparison and logical operators

A condition is an expression that produces a [[Boolean]]. [[Comparison Operators]] covers the
six operators that produce one: `==` for equal, `!=` for different, and `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`
for ordering. A single `=` assigns a value and a double `==` compares two, and confusing them
is the standard early mistake.

[[Logical Operators]] covers `not`, `and`, `or`, which combine conditions. `and` is `True`
when both sides are, `or` is `True` when at least one side is, and `not` inverts a single
value. They evaluate in that order of precedence, so `not` binds tightest and `or` binds
loosest, and brackets override it.

These operators short-circuit, which is a technique to use deliberately. Python stops
evaluating as soon as the answer is settled, so in the condition below the division never
executes when `count` is zero:

```python
if count != 0 and total / count > 10:
```

The guard and the operation it guards sit in one condition, and the order of the two halves is
what makes it safe. These are the AND, OR and NOT of [[Boolean Algebra]], and De Morgan's laws
apply to them exactly as they apply to a circuit.

### Making decisions

[[Descision]] and [[Conditional]] cover `if`, `elif` and `else`, which choose between blocks
of code based on a condition.

```python
if mark >= 80:
    grade = "A"
elif mark >= 70:
    grade = "B"
else:
    grade = "C"
```

The branches are tested in order and the first true one runs, so the ordering of the
conditions is part of the logic. [[Dangling else]] and [[Switch]] are C constructs that
Python's indentation rules and `elif` keyword make impossible to write.

### Repeating work

A loop runs the same block of code more than once. [[Repetition]] covers the idea, and the two
forms differ in what they know at the start. A [[While loop]] repeats while a condition holds
and needs no idea how many iterations that will take. A [[For loop]] walks through a
collection of values and takes one iteration per value.

```python
total = 0
for number in [4, 8, 15]:
    total += number        # total ends at 27
```

That `total` is an [[Accumulator]], the running-total pattern that augmented assignment is the
notation for. A [[Control variable]] in a while loop has to be initialised before the loop,
tested in the condition, and updated inside the body. Omitting the update produces an
[[Infinite loop]], where the condition never becomes false and the program never moves on.
[[Counted loop]] and [[Finite loop]] cover loops that know their iteration count in advance,
[[Sentinel]] covers a loop that stops when a marker value appears, and [[Loop design]] is the
checklist for building one. [[Nested loop]] covers a loop inside another loop, which is what a
grid needs.

Everything in this section is owned by [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] and transfers
between the two languages with no change beyond syntax.

### Functions

A [[Function]] is a named block of code that can be run from anywhere by using its name. It
takes values in, does its work, and hands a value back.

```python
def area(width, height):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))          # prints 12
```

Functions exist so a problem can be split into pieces that are solved and tested separately,
and so a piece of logic is written once and used repeatedly. The values named in the
definition are the [[Formal parameter|formal parameters]], the values supplied by the caller
are the [[Actual parameter|actual parameters]], and [[Parameter]] covers the general idea.
Functions split into the ones that return a value and the ones that work purely by their
effects, and [[Void]] in COMP 1633 covers the second kind.

[[Variable Scope]] is where a name is visible. A variable created inside a function exists
only while that function runs, so two functions can use the name `total` without interfering
with each other.

[[Docstring]] is the text in triple quotes on the first line of the function body, and it is
more than a comment. The string survives into the running program, so `help(area)` prints it
at the interpreter. [[Standard Library]] covers the modules Python ships with, including
`math` and `random`, plus `turtle` for graphics, and [[Library]] covers importing them. The
`random` module is a seeded pseudo-random generator, so the same seed produces the same
sequence and a program using it stays reproducible, which [[Random Numbers]] in
[[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] explains in full.

### Lists

A [[Python List]] holds many values under one name, in order. Each value has a position called
an [[Index]], counting from 0.

```python
names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan"]
print(names[0])            # Ada
print(names[-1])           # Alan, counting from the right
print(names[0:2])          # ["Ada", "Grace"], a slice
names.append("Edsger")     # the list grows on demand
```

A Python list grows as needed, holds values of mixed types, accepts a negative index to count
backwards, supports slicing to take a section, and raises `IndexError` on a position that
does not exist. The equivalent in C is the [[Array]], which is faster, fixed in size, and
reads whatever byte happens to sit at an out-of-range address. [[List]] in COMP 1633 covers
the list as an [[Abstract Data Type]], meaning the set of operations it offers, separately
from the [[Implementation]] that provides them.

One behaviour surprises everyone. `b = a` gives the same list a second name, so a change made
through one name is visible through the other. `b = a[:]` copies it.

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)                # a is now [1, 2, 3, 4] as well
```

That is [[Call by reference]] arriving a year early, and COMP 1633 explains the mechanism.

### Two-dimensional lists

A list can hold other lists, which is how a grid is represented. Each inner list is one row,
and two indices reach a single value, the first choosing the row and the second choosing the
position within it.

```python
grid = [[1, 2, 3],
        [4, 5, 6]]

print(grid[1][2])          # 6, second row, third column
print(len(grid))           # 2 rows
print(len(grid[0]))        # 3 columns
```

Visiting every cell takes a [[Nested loop]], with the outer loop walking the rows and the inner
loop walking the positions in the current row:

```python
for row in grid:
    for value in row:
        print(value)
```

The rows are separate lists, so they can hold different numbers of values. Building one with
`[ [0] * 3 ] * 2` produces two names for the same row, so writing into one row appears to write
into both. A grid is built with a loop or a comprehension for that reason. This structure is how a game
board, a spreadsheet and an image are all stored, and [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] studies the same
arrangement as a [[Matrix]].

### Classes and objects

A class groups data together with the functions that work on that data. This course introduces
the idea and [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] develops it in full.

A [[Class]] is the definition, describing what every instance will hold and what it can do. An
[[Object]] is one instance built from that definition, holding its own values. A function
defined inside a class is a [[Method]], and it receives the object it was called on as its
first parameter, named `self`.

```python
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, mark):
        self.name = name
        self.mark = mark

    def passed(self):
        return self.mark >= 50

evan = Student("Evan", 87)
print(evan.name)           # Evan
print(evan.passed())       # True
```

Everything above could be written with a plain variable for the name and a separate function
taking that name as an argument. The class keeps the data and the operations on it in one
place, so code elsewhere in the program uses `evan.passed()` without knowing how a mark is
stored. That is [[Abstraction]], and restricting outside access to the stored values is
[[Encapsulation]]. [[Classes]] carries the fuller treatment.

### Files

[[File I-O]] is how a program reads and writes data that outlives it. The sequence is open the
file, process it, close it, and the `with` statement performs the close automatically.

```python
with open("marks.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())
```

Two details catch everyone. Every value read from a [[File]] arrives as a [[String]], so a
number read from a file needs converting before arithmetic. Each line keeps the newline
character at its end, which is what `strip()` removes above. Opening a file in mode `"w"`
empties it immediately, before anything is written.

### Errors, testing and debugging

[[Errors]] holds the taxonomy, and the three kinds differ in when they are noticed.
[[Compile Errors]] are reported before the code runs, which in Python means the parser
rejecting a syntax mistake. [[Runtime Errors]] stop the program partway through, such as
dividing by zero or indexing past the end of a list. [[Logic Errors]] are never reported by
anything: the program runs to completion and produces the wrong answer.

Python has no compile step, so the type mismatches a C++ compiler rejects before running
appear here as runtime errors, and a branch that never executes can hold one indefinitely.

[[Test Coverage]] answers the question [[Unit testing]] and [[Driver]] leave open, which is
which inputs to test. Split the possible inputs into groups that should behave the same way
and test one value from each, then test every boundary and the value on each side of it. The
difference between `>` and `>=` is invisible at 75 and immediately visible at 50. [[debugging]]
covers working backwards from a failure to the line that caused it, and a [[Tracing Table]] is
the tool when there is no error message to read.

## Where the notes live

Most of what this course teaches has its note in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]],
written in [[C]] a year later, including variables, functions, scope, decisions, loops,
errors, lists and files. That reflects when the vault was started. The notes in this folder
are the ones belonging to Python specifically or to neither language.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) is the sequel and owns most of this
  material in [[C]], including [[Variable]], [[Function]], [[Variable Scope]],
  [[Data type]], [[Descision]], [[Repetition]], [[Errors]], [[List]], [[Array]] and
  [[File]]. It repeats these ideas with the machine visible, so [[Pointer]], [[Memory]],
  [[Stack and Heap]] and [[Dynamic Allocation]] show what Python was hiding.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) asks what a list costs, which this course
  deliberately leaves alone. See [[Time Complexity]], [[Linked List]] and [[Hashing]].
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) takes [[Hardware]], [[Processor]] and
  [[Machine Language]] seriously, and treats [[C]] as the translation layer between a
  language and the hardware.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] (COMP 2633) gives [[Unit testing]] and
  [[Coupling and Cohesion]] their full treatment, and develops the class into a way of
  designing a whole system.
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] (COMP 3649) starts from the fact that functions are values, which
  is true in Python and central in [[Haskell]].
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) and [[MACHINE LEARNING]] are where Python
  returns as the working language of the degree.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] covers [[Random Numbers]], and opens with the properties an
  [[Algorithm]] has to have.
- [[SYMBOLIC LOGIC]] (PHIL 1179) defines the operators [[Logical Operators]] implements, and
  explains why `and` and `or` behave as they do.
